title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Incident Reviews, Tooling, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Purpose
This page captures Redwood Inference SRE standards for service level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. The goal is to provide a single, actionable reference for service owners, on-call engineers, and platform SREs.

Scope
Applies to all customer-facing inference services (API, routing, model-serving), control-plane components (auth, billing, telemetry), and internal infra that directly impacts SLOs. Components that are strictly developer tooling may follow a lighter-weight variant of these standards per product agreement.

Key definitions
- SLI (Service Level Indicator): a measured metric such as request success rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, or embedding correctness for a given route.
- SLO (Service Level Objective): a target on an SLI (e.g., availability 99.95% over 30d).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO. The allowable fraction of bad behavior before corrective action is required.
- Burn rate: speed at which the error budget is being consumed relative to the time window.

Section 1: SLO and Error Budget Standards
1.1 SLO design principles - SLOs must reflect customer-visible quality (latency and availability are primary for inference routes).
- Keep SLOs simple: prefer a small set (2–4) of SLIs per service: availability, latency (p95/p99), and correctness for high-risk model outputs.
- Use the longest reasonable rolling window aligned with product risk: 30d default for availability; 7d for high-change services (canary, model rollouts).
- Define SLOs per logical route or tier (e.g., /v1/generate-high-priority, embeddings-fast, control-plane).

1.2 Recommended SLOs (examples)
- API availability: 99.95% (30d window) for hosted inference routes.
- P95 latency: <= 1200ms for text-generation (configurable by model class).
- P99 latency: <= 2500ms for text-generation routes.
- Embeddings: 99.9% availability, p95 <= 300ms.

1.3 Error budget policy and actions
- Green (burn rate < 1): continue normal operations.
- Yellow (burn rate between 1 and 4): schedule immediate triage, pause non-essential launches and non-urgent infra changes, increase monitoring granularity.
- Red (burn rate >= 4): execute emergency throttling and protective actions, notify stakeholders, and require a remediation plan within 2 business hours.
Required actions table (text table)
| Burn state | Burn rate | Required actions | Owner |
|------------|-----------|------------------|-------|
| Green | < 1 | Normal ops | Service owner |
| Yellow | 1 - 4 | Triage, freeze non-essential changes, increase sampling | On-call engineer, service owner |
| Red | >= 4 | Emergency throttles, fallback routing, exec notification, incident if needed | SRE Lead, Product Ops |

1.4 SLO ownership and review cadence
- Service owners must publish SLOs in their service README and register them in the SLO registry (internal dashboard).
- Quarterly SLO review with product/PM, engineering, and SRE to validate risk/targets.
- Any change to an SLO requires a documented rationale and a two-week rolling observation period before reclassification.

Section 2: Capacity Planning
2.1 Capacity model
- Components: baseline throughput, peak-to-average ratio, headroom margin (default 30%), and safety buffer for model rollouts (default +20% per major rollout).
- Forecast inputs: usage growth (weekly), recent rollouts, marketing events, regional expansion, and historical p99 latency shifts.

2.2 Forecasting cadence and owners
- Weekly short-term (7–14 days) forecast maintained by capacity SRE.
- Monthly medium-term (90 days) forecast aligned with product roadmap and customer commitments.
- Quarterly long-term planning (12 months) for procurement and major hardware purchases.

2.3 Autoscaling and burst policies
- Autoscaling targets: keep p95 latency within SLO at target traffic with safety buffer.
- Burst capacity: configured per pool with a maximum burst multiplier (default 1.5x) and a maximum burst duration (default 10 minutes) before shedding or queuing.
- Pre-warming: for scheduled marketing or enterprise events, request pre-warm at least 72 hours in advance.

2.4 Capacity runbook checklist
- Validate recent traffic trend and model composition.
- Verify available GPU pool and instance types.
- Confirm autoscaler healthy and target utilization between 55–75%.
- Run smoke tests against representative inference routes.

Section 3: Reliability Initiatives and Program Governance
3.1 Initiative intake template
- Title
- Owner
- Problem statement and customer impact
- Success criteria (quantitative; tie to SLO improvement or cost reduction)
- Timeline and key milestones
- Rollout plan and rollback criteria

3.2 Prioritization
- Prioritize initiatives that: reduce customer-facing incidents, materially extend error budget life, or reduce unit cost while preserving SLOs.
- Use Quarterly Reliability OKRs and a cross-functional intake board (SRE, product, infra) for approvals.

3.3 Measuring impact
- Required metrics: change in SLI, error budget burn improvement, incident count/frequency, mean time to restore (MTTR), and cost-per-token (where applicable).

Section 4: Incident Review and Postmortem Standards
4.1 Severity taxonomy (brief)
- Sev1: partial/complete outage of critical customer paths (>5% customer impact or sustained degradation >30 minutes).
- Sev2: significant degradation of key SLOs (<5% customer impact or sustained degradation >30 minutes).
- Sev3: minor impact, degraded non-critical paths, or internal tooling incidents.

4.2 Postmortem requirements
- Timeline: initial incident review within 48 hours; full postmortem published within 7 calendar days for Sev1/Sev2, 14 days for Sev3 (expedited for customer-facing escalations).
- Content: impact summary, timeline, root cause analysis (RCA), contributing factors, detection and mitigation timeline, remediation plan (owner and due date), and learnings.
- Blameless language: focus on systemic fixes, avoid naming individuals as root cause.

4.3 Review process and enforcement
- Postmortems must be reviewed in a weekly reliability review meeting.
- Action items tracked in the reliability board; overdue actions escalate to SRE Lead.
- Repeat incidents require root-cause re-evaluation and a deeper corrective plan (e.g., design change).

Section 5: Operational Tooling and Observability Standards
5.1 Monitoring and alerting
- Metrics required for all services: request success rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, request rate, CPU/GPU utilization, queue/backlog length, and error categories.
- Alerting rules: combine symptom alerts (high latency, increased error rates) with cause alerts (disk pressure, autoscaler failures). Use paged alerts for likely customer-impacting conditions only.
- Alert thresholds: tuned to maximize actionable signals; target < 3 false positives per pager per week per on-call.

5.2 Dashboards and SLO visibility
- SLO dashboard: time-series of SLIs and error budget burn with burn-rate annotations and recent incidents.
- Runbook links must be embedded on dashboards for rapid access.

5.3 Observability tooling list (approved)
- Metrics: Prometheus/OpenMetrics + remote write to central TSDB.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry + sampled traces for long tails.
- Logs: centralized ELK/Graylog with index retention aligned to incident needs (90 days baseline).
- SLO & error budget: internal SLO service (dashboard + alerting integrations).

Section 6: Canonical SRE Runbooks (examples)
6.1 Runbook: High p95/p99 latency on generation route (/v1/generate)
Purpose: Steps to diagnose and mitigate elevated latency for generation routes.
Owner: service owner and on-call SRE
Severity threshold to run: service p95 > 1200ms for > 3 minutes or p99 > 2500ms for > 2 minutes.
Steps:
1) Triage and initial checks (0-5 minutes)
   - Check SLO dashboard and recent deploys.
   - Confirm error budget state and burn rate.
   - Verify autoscaler health and target utilization.
   - Check GPU pool health, instance replacement events, and elevated host load.
2) Narrow down cause (5-15 minutes)
   - Inspect traces for tail latency causes (large sequence lengths, KV cache misses).
   - Check model composition: any recent model variant rollouts or quantization changes.
   - Check for network saturation, AZ failures, or egress throttling.
3) Mitigations (15-60 minutes)
   - If autoscaler lagging, trigger manual scale-up for affected pools.
   - Rollback recent model variant if correlated with latency increase.
   - Enable fallback to lower-latency model variant or increase batching policy temporarily.
   - If due to KV cache cold starts, prioritize cache warm-up and limit new large-context requests.
4) Communication and follow-up
   - Notify product and support teams with impact statement and ETA.
   - Open incident and assign postmortem owner if burn state became Yellow+ or customer impact observed.

6.2 Runbook: Error rate spike (5xx) on control-plane (/v1/auth)
Purpose: Contain and remediate service errors impacting customer auth/management paths.
Owner: control-plane service owner and SRE
Steps:
1) Immediate containment
   - Check recent deploys and rollout flags.
   - If new deploy present, rollback to last known-good.
   - If DB connectivity errors observed, reroute to failover DB and scale read replicas.
2) Diagnosis
   - Correlate error codes with upstream dependencies.
   - Check config changes (feature flags, rate-limiter thresholds).
3) Remediation and post-incident
   - Patch and redeploy with fixed config, then validate under load.
   - Write postmortem and remedial actions.

Section 7: Runbook and Playbook Hygiene
- Owners must keep runbooks < 2 pages and focused on actionable steps and links to diagnostics.
- Every runbook must include: purpose, owner, severity threshold, step-by-step mitigation, escalation path, and required dashboard links.
- Review runbooks quarterly and after every Sev1/Sev2 incident.

Appendix: Templates
- Postmortem template (headline fields): incident id, severity, detection time, mitigation time, impact, timeline, root cause, contributing factors, corrective actions (owner + due date), follow-up reviews.
- Runbook template (headline fields): title, purpose, owner, severity threshold, diagnostic commands, mitigation steps, escalation contacts, post-incident tasks.

Frequently asked questions (FAQ)
Q: When should we tighten SLOs?
A: Tighten SLOs only after sustained error budget surpluses and validated capacity/architecture improvements; always perform a two-week observational window.

Q: Who approves emergency throttle/mitigation for multi-tenant pools?
A: SRE Lead + product owner for the impacted route; if customer-facing SLA risks exist, notify Customer Success immediately.
